content: The SOS1 gene encodes a protein known as Son of Sevenless Homolog 1 in humans. This protein plays a critical role in cellular signaling pathways that regulate cell growth and differentiation. RAS genes encode guanine nucleotide-binding proteins that are anchored to the cell membrane. These proteins are essential for transmitting signals that control cellular growth and differentiation. RAS proteins are activated when they bind to guanosine triphosphate (GTP). This activation is reversed when the bound GTP is hydrolyzed to guanosine diphosphate (GDP) and inorganic phosphate, which inactivates the signaling function of RAS proteins. The exchange of GDP for GTP on RAS proteins is facilitated by guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs), while the hydrolysis of GTP is accelerated by GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs). The first guanine nucleotide exchange factor identified for RAS was the CDC25 gene product in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Genetic studies demonstrated that CDC25 is essential for the activation of RAS proteins. In Drosophila, the protein encoded by the son of sevenless (Sos) gene contains a domain that is structurally similar to the catalytic domain of CDC25. This suggests that Sos functions as a positive regulator of RAS by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. Mutations in the SOS1 gene have been implicated in certain medical conditions. For example, mutations in SOS1 can lead to Noonan syndrome, a genetic disorder characterized by distinctive facial features, short stature, congenital heart defects, and other abnormalities. Additionally, mutations in SOS1 have been associated with hereditary gingival fibromatosis type 1, a condition characterized by excessive growth of the gum tissue. Noonan syndrome can also result from mutations in other genes, such as KRAS and PTPN11, which are involved in the activation of the MAP kinase signaling pathway. The SOS1 protein has been shown to interact with several other proteins, including: ABI1 (Abl interactor 1), The BCR gene product, CRK (an adaptor protein), EPS8 (epidermal growth factor receptor pathway substrate 8), Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), FRS2 (fibroblast growth factor receptor substrate 2), Grb2 (growth factor receptor-bound protein 2), HRAS (a member of the RAS family), ITSN1 (intersectin 1), MUC1 (mucin 1), NCK1 (an adaptor protein), PLCG1 (phospholipase C gamma 1), PTPN11 (protein tyrosine phosphatase non-receptor type 11), SH3KBP1 (SH3 domain-containing kinase-binding protein 1), and SHC1 (SHC-transforming protein 1). These interactions highlight the central role of SOS1 in various signaling pathways that regulate cellular processes.
